title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks (Standards)
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning methodology, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers who operate or onboard production services.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing services (hosted API, control plane, console, telemetry pipeline) and core internal services that impact customer-facing SLAs.
- Excludes one-off experimental services which must be onboarded to this standard before production use.

Goals:
- Provide consistent, measurable SLOs with actionable error budget policies.
- Ensure capacity planning avoids sustained degradation and supports business growth.
- Standardize incident reviews and runbooks to reduce time-to-recovery and improve blameless postmortems.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO Principles:
- Define SLOs that reflect customer experience (availability, correctness, latency) not implementation details.
- Keep SLOs simple: primary SLOs (availability, latency) + one secondary SLO where required (e.g., correctness for ranking/embedding services).
- Target SLOs should be aligned with product tiers (free, standard, enterprise).

Required SLOs (recommended defaults):
- Availability SLI: successful 2xx responses / total requests. Default SLO: 99.9% (monthly) for standard tier; 99.95% for enterprise-critical endpoints.
- Latency SLI: end-to-end request latency measured at edge (ingress -> response). Default SLOs: p50 < 40ms, p95 < 250ms, p99 < 600ms for text-generation endpoints (varies by model/sequence length).
- Correctness SLI (where applicable): model outputs passing curated prompt-set checks or evaluation harness acceptance criteria. Default SLO: 98% passing for critical classification endpoints.

Error Budget Policy:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Track burn-rate over rolling 14-day and 28-day windows.
- Burn thresholds and actions (automated where possible):
  1. Green (burn_rate <= 1.0): Normal ops. Continue planned rollouts.
  2. Elevated (1.0 < burn_rate <= 4.0): Pause non-critical feature rollouts; notify product and platform.
  3. High (4.0 < burn_rate <= 10.0): Halt all deploys; escalate to SRE on-call; run targeted mitigations.
  4. Critical (burn_rate > 10.0 or sustained > 4.0 for 24h): Emergency response; invoke incident playbook and exec notify.
- Error budget consumption should be published weekly to owners and product managers; monthly executive summaries for enterprise customers.

SLO Ownership and Reviews:
- Each SLO must list a primary owner (service owner) and an SRE reviewer. Owners are responsible for alerting, dashboards, and remediation playbooks.
- Quarterly SLO reviews: validate SLOs against customer expectations and cost tradeoffs. Document review outcomes in linked change log.

2) Capacity Planning

Capacity planning cadence:
- Quarterly capacity review with the following inputs: traffic growth forecasts, model/sequence length trends, feature rollout calendar, upcoming enterprise commitments, and reliability metrics.
- Monthly operational check-ins for near-term burst planning.

Capacity model:
- Demand = baseline QPS * expected growth multiplier + scheduled burst allowances. Capture variability: 95th and 99th percentile QPS over historical windows (7/30/90 days).
- Headroom target: Maintain 20% spare GPU vCPU and network capacity for normal operations, 40% for enterprise-critical services.
- Autoscaling: prefer horizontal scaling of stateless frontends and routing tiers; use instance pools with pre-warmed VMs for GPU-backed inference.
- Warmup: pre-warm model instances for scheduled releases and enterprise rollouts (see Runbook: Planned Release).

Capacity runbook checklist (quarterly):
1. Export traffic and latency percentiles (7/30/90d).
2. Re-run cost/throughput model per model profile and quantization setting.
3. Validate autoscaler policies (scale-up/down thresholds, cooldowns).
4. Confirm N-day commit capacity with finance for Dedicated customers.
5. Update playbooks and dashboards where thresholds change.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Program Structure

Program structure:
- Reliability initiatives (RIs) are 6-12 week projects that target measurable SLO improvement or cost/stability wins (e.g., caching, batching, kernel tuning).
- Each RI must include: objective (metric target), owner, experiment plan, rollback criteria, measurement plan (metrics & dashboards), and a short executive summary.

Examples of priority initiatives:
- KV/Prefix caching for embedding and chat sessions to reduce token compute by 25%.
- Adaptive batching improvements to reduce p95 latency by 15% under steady load.
- Automated quantization profile rollout for cold-start models to cut cost by 30% with <1% regression on correctness SLI.

Tracking and measurement:
- Use a reliability scorecard per service: SLO attainment, error budget burn rate, MTTR, change failure rate, and cost per 1M tokens. Report monthly.

4) Incident Review Standards

Incident classification:
- Sev0 (SEV0): Customer-facing outage impacting >5% of traffic or enterprise SLA breach. Immediate exec notification; war room.
- Sev1: Degraded service for >1% traffic or significant latency regressions. Escalate to SRE on-call.
- Sev2/3: Localized issues or non-critical degradations; handled by on-call with post-incident follow-up.

Postmortem requirements (for Sev0/1):
- Timeliness: draft within 48 hours, final within 7 days.
- Template: summary, timeline, impact, root cause, detection and mitigation steps, corrective actions (short/medium/long-term), owners, and follow-up verification plan.
- Blamelessness: focus on systems and process failure. Avoid naming individuals.
- Severity justification: include metrics showing customer impact and error budget consumption.
- Action item tracking: create tasks in the engineering tracker and link them to the incident page; verify completion within agreed SLAs (short-term within 7 days, long-term within 90 days).

Incident review forum:
- Weekly reliability review meeting to triage high-burn or recurring incidents and approve RIs. Invite service owners and relevant PMs.

5) Operational Tooling

Monitoring and alerts:
- Primary telemetry: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and structured logs ingested into our observability stack (Grafana, Tempo, Loki).
- Alerting policy: alerts must map to runbook playbooks; use RTT (recovery time to threshold) labels and enrich alerts with runbook links.
- Alert noise threshold: no more than 3 actionable alerts per on-call per hour from a single service under normal operations. Use alert deduping and grouping.

Dashboards and runbooks:
- Every SLO must have a dashboard with: SLO graph, burn-rate windows (14/28d), top contributing errors by tag, latency histograms, and capacity utilization.
- Runbooks should be one-click linked from alerts and explain immediate mitigation steps, owner contacts, and escalation path.

Tooling examples (PromQL snippets and commands):
- Availability SLI (PromQL):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",status!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

- Error budget burn-rate (14d):
  (1 - (sum_over_time(successful_requests[14d]) / sum_over_time(total_requests[14d]))) / (1 - target_slo)

- Alerting example (Grafana/Alertmanager):
  - alert: HighErrorBudgetBurn
    expr: error_budget_burn_rate_14d > 4
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "High error budget burn for {{ $labels.service }}"
      runbook: "https://confluence.internal/eng-sre/runbooks/{{ $labels.service }}-incident"

6) SRE Runbooks (Canonical Playbooks)

Runbook: High-latency spike (API p95 > target)
1. Triage (first 10 minutes):
   - Check SLO dashboard and burn-rate windows.
   - Run: kubectl get pods -l app={{service}} -n prod; check pod restarts and OOMs.
   - Inspect recent deployments: link to CI job and rollout timeline.
2. Immediate mitigations (10-30 minutes):
   - If CPU/GPU saturation: scale out replicas or increase GPU pool for inference nodes (use pre-warmed instances).
   - If new deployment correlated: rollback to previous stable revision.
   - If queue/backpressure: increase workers or throttle low-priority traffic.
3. Stabilize (30-120 minutes):
   - Validate p95/p99 and confirm traffic returns to baseline.
   - Document mitigations in incident log.
4. Follow-up:
   - Create action items for capacity or code fixes.
   - Schedule blameless postmortem if SEV1/0.

Runbook: OOMs / GPU OOM or memory pressure
1. Triage:
   - Check node memory/persistent GPU metrics.
   - Identify which model variant or quantization profile caused memory spike.
2. Immediate mitigation:
   - Reduce batch size or switch to a lower-memory model variant.
   - If out-of-capacity: re-route traffic to compatible region or fallback model.
3. Long-term:
   - Add guardrails in admission/controller to enforce safe batch sizes.
   - Add automated tests in CI to detect memory regressions for model changes.

Runbook: Degraded worker pool / queue backlog
1. Check: queue length, consumer lag, and worker instance health.
2. Action: temporarily scale consumers, reduce ingestion rate, or toggle feature flags for non-critical paths.
3. If persistent: investigate root cause (consumer leak, DB latency) and create RI.

7) Onboarding and Documentation Requirements

Onboarding checklist for new services:
- Define SLOs and list owners (service + SRE).
- Create dashboards and alerts per SLO.
- Provide runbooks for the Top-3 failure modes.
- Provide capacity model inputs and quarterly review schedule.
- Link to compliance/enterprise contracts if applicable.

Documentation formatting and storage:
- Use Confluence pages under confluence/eng-sre with the following sections: Overview, SLOs, Dashboards, Alerts, Runbooks, Capacity Plan, Incidents & Postmortems, Related Pages.
- Keep runbooks concise (one page preferred) with clear step-by-step mitigation; link to deeper debugging docs where needed.

8) Metrics, Reporting, and KPIs

Primary KPIs reported monthly:
- SLO attainment per service (monthly and rolling 28d).
- MTTR (median and p95) per severity class.
- Error budget burn rate trends.
- Change failure rate and rollout success rate.
- Cost per 1M tokens and cost per 1000 requests (tracked by model profile).

9) Governance and Continuous Improvement

- SRE Council: monthly review of high-burn services and approval of large RIs.
- Retrospectives: perform 6-12 week reviews on completed RIs to capture learnings.
- Continuous documentation: update this page after any policy or tooling change; maintain a changelog.

Appendices:
A. Postmortem template (copy-paste-ready):
- Title:
- SEV: 
- Start / End time:
- Impact summary (customers affected, query volume impacted):
- Timeline (UTC):
- Root cause:

- Short/medium/long term actions (owner + due date):
- Verification plan:
- Lessons learned:

B. Quick PromQL snippets (copyable):
- p95 latency (ms): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le)) * 1000
- pod restarts (24h): increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="prod",pod=~"{{service}}.*"}[24h])
